title: A 2,200-Year-Old Shipwreck's Sticky Secret
summary:
A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

For as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive damage. Yet until the mid-20th century, studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden parts, and the protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention.

In a new study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Parzine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank about 2,200 years ago. The shipwreck was discovered in 2016, and this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both what the coatings were made of and what plants grew nearby when they were produced or applied.

"In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," said first author Dr. Armelle Charrie, an archaeometrist in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax."

The team analysed 10 samples of the coating. Distinctive chemical signatures showed that the main waterproofing material was pitch made from heated conifer resin or tar, a thick, sticky substance used for centuries to seal wooden vessels. One sample, however, contained a different recipe: pine tar combined with beeswax, a mixture known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa. The beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to apply while hot, a valuable property aboard wooden ships whose timbers shift and flex in waves.

The sticky pitch had another remarkable property that ancient shipbuilders probably never considered: it could capture tiny airborne pollen grains and preserve them for thousands of years. Different plants produce pollen with distinctive shapes, so scientists could identify the vegetation present long after the plants themselves had disappeared. The pollen pointed to Mediterranean and Adriatic coastal areas, forests of holly oak and pine, shrubland with olive and hazel trees, and fir and beech from mountainous areas, a mix characteristic of the northeastern Adriatic coast.
why_it_matters: This discovery shows how clever ancient builders were, and how science can read clues from tiny pollen grains to rebuild the story of a ship that sailed more than 2,000 years ago.

background_read: Wooden ships need protection from the sea, because salt water and sea creatures can rot and damage wood.
Archaeologists study old wrecks to learn how people built ships and lived long ago.
Pollen is the fine dust plants release, and different plants make pollen with different shapes.
Because sticky coatings can trap pollen for thousands of years, scientists can use it like a time capsule of the plants that grew nearby.
